ami_style_notes:
The meeting has a casual, collegial videoconference style, with mostly short-to-medium turns outside the presentations and long, structured monologues during talks. The opening is loose and overlapping, full of greetings, technical checks, side chatter, repetitions, false starts, and fillers such as “yeah,” “um,” “okay,” and “right”; speakers often self-correct or restart mid-sentence. Formality is low to moderate: participants use first names, compliments, teasing, and conversational asides, but shift into more formal, appreciative language for introductions and questions. Questions are typically prefaced with praise or hedges (“great talk,” “I have a naive question,” “I’m just curious”), then develop through several follow-ups rather than one cleanly phrased prompt. Challenges are indirect and exploratory, framed as uncertainty or alternative possibilities rather than disagreement. Speakers build on one another by paraphrasing prior points, checking understanding, and adding related examples; answers are generous and tentative, often acknowledging limits, open questions, and future work.

Meeting style for this meeting (round_robin_updates): Each person takes a turn reporting what they have done since last time. Updates are fairly long and mostly uninterrupted. There are a few clarifying questions between updates and little cross-talk. The discussion that does happen is brief.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - Okay, mine. I got through most of the interviews, I think fourteen of twenty, and the rest are scheduled for the following two weeks.
  - Fourteen, nice. Were those all from the first batch?
  - Most of them. A couple were referrals.
Opening: Start with a person asking for a quick catch-up because they missed the last meeting.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Reducing 30-day hospital readmissions for older adults with heart failure after they go home.

speakers.name: Dr. Maya Chen
speakers.background: A geriatric cardiology fellow and health-services PhD candidate with 6 years of inpatient and transitional-care experience. She has led chart-abstraction and electronic health record cohort studies of heart-failure discharges, focusing on guideline-directed medical therapy, medication reconciliation discrepancies, pharmacy fill data, and 30-day all-cause readmission. She will coordinate the clinical implementation specifications and outcome-data plan with the hospital analytics team.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Frames the program as a transitional-care intervention whose credibility depends on a reproducible discharge workflow and prespecified clinical endpoints. She emphasizes identifying eligible heart-failure discharges, documenting medication reconciliation and follow-up contact fidelity, and linking those processes to all-cause 30-day readmissions, guideline-directed therapy, and medication adherence. She confirms that the intervention and clinical outcome-data plan can proceed once approvals and hospital data access are in place.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

speakers.name: Dr. Rafael Morales
speakers.background: A medical sociologist with 14 years of experience studying chronic illness, care work, and institutional trust among older adults and families. His mixed-methods work combines semistructured interviews, ethnographic field notes, household mapping, and limited home-based observation to examine how discharge plans are enacted amid caregiving obligations, transportation constraints, language access, and prior encounters with health institutions. He is the study's principal investigator and leads the qualitative protocol and fieldwork training.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Treats readmission risk not only as an individual adherence problem but as an outcome produced through household labor, unequal access to support, and trust-mediated decisions about when and where to seek care. He specifies that participant interviews and limited home-based observations require institutional review approval. Interview recruitment, consent, scheduling, and fieldwork are planned to start on February 1, 2027, and he will use those encounters to characterize caregiving arrangements and trust in the health system.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

speakers.name: Dr. Aisha Patel
speakers.background: A health economist with 11 years of experience evaluating hospital-based care-management programs, Medicare payment incentives, and post-acute utilization. She builds micro-costing models from staff time, training, information-technology use, and community-navigation inputs, then links these estimates to claims and hospital service-use data for cost-effectiveness and budget-impact analyses. Her prior work has examined how readmission penalties and alternative payment arrangements change hospitals' financial incentives.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Assesses whether the support program is implementable at a cost that is defensible under hospital readmission-penalty and payment models, rather than assuming that fewer readmissions automatically produce savings. She emphasizes that costing depends on a finalized intervention workflow and on service-use and readmission data, including staff effort, referral intensity, and avoidable versus shifted utilization. She does not treat economic modeling as a mechanism for settling the approval schedule.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Patel
transcript.text: Hi, everyone. Before we start, I missed the end of the last meeting—the tail end, I mean. Did anything substantive change on the workflow, or was it mostly submission logistics? For today, I was hoping we could do a quick round on where things stand, especially the clinical contact workflow and what data access is looking like, since those are the pieces I need before the costing model is more than a placeholder.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Mostly logistics. Clinically, the workflow is still the same. We screen eligible heart-failure discharges, complete and document reconciliation, then do the post-discharge contact. I’m waiting on the approvals and hospital analytics access before we can validate the extraction. One thing I’m checking is whether pharmacy-fill linkage will arrive fast enough to support the adherence measure, rather than just being retrospective- sorry, retrospective only.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Patel
transcript.text: Maya, for the contact workflow, will the documentation retain unsuccessful call attempts and any escalation or referral-follow-up time, not just the completed reconciliation and contact? Those are often where the labor-cost variation sits, and they can be pretty invisible if the extract is built around completed contacts— encounters.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: We need to retain all of that at the encounter level, each attempted call, whether someone was reached, duration if feasible, escalation, and whether a community or pharmacy referral was actually closed. Otherwise the workflow will look artificially frictionless, and I agree, Aisha, staffing records won’t reconstruct those patient-specific failures very well...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Morales
transcript.text: That level of encounter detail will matter qualitatively too, because an unsuccessful contact can reflect household schedules, language mediation, or just reluctance to re-engage after a difficult discharge. Maya, for the all-cause readmissions, how much of that pre-return sequence is actually recoverable from the record? Like symptom onset, who made the decision, whether they tried calling first, or is it mostly just the admission endpoint?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: It’s mostly the admission endpoint, honestly. We can reliably get the return date, diagnosis, utilization, and sometimes ED notes or a documented outreach attempt. But the decision pathway before they came back is patchy and would need a targeted abstraction, not just a standard extract. Rafael, the household account may be the only way to understand whether they tried to manage symptoms or medications at home before that, um, threshold was crossed.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Morales
transcript.text: And I wouldn't assume the household account just fills in a factual gap in the chart. The preliminary listening suggests trust and help-seeking aren't linear. Some families who felt well supported still waited, while others with very negative prior encounters sought help almost immediately. So the interviews can reconstruct the sequence, but also how they interpreted symptoms, how they, um, took on care work for each other, and how they decided whether calling was the right thing to do.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Patel
transcript.text: That distinction is useful for me too, because navigation intensity may be responding to really different things, like lack of an available caregiver, limited household resources, or reluctance to use the system. Rafael, from the interviews, do you think we can tell which of those is driving the referral work, at least in broad- broader categories? Otherwise, a high-touch case just looks expensive without telling us why.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Morales
transcript.text: I think we can develop broad categories that are analytically useful, but I’d resist treating them as mutually exclusive drivers. The interviews and the household map can distinguish, say, unavailable care labor, transport or benefits barriers, language mediation, and different forms of institutional mistrust, while still showing how they co-produce the referral work. Assuming approval is in hand, we’d start recruitment and consent on February 1, 2027, so we can refine those categories before April enrollment.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: That would help a lot, especially if the household map makes clear who is actually administering or organizing medications day to day. One thing I need us to anticipate is disagreement. In a small discharge audit, we had completed reconciliation and calls, but the first outpatient medication list still differed from- diverged from the discharge list. If the patient and caregiver give different versions of who changed what, how would you want to capture that?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Morales
transcript.text: I'd treat the discrepancy itself as data rather than trying to adjudicate it immediately. In the interview, we can ask each person separately, where feasible, who understood a change had been made, by whom, and what prompted it. The household map can then show who had practical authority over the medicines versus who was expected to remember the plan. We should also preserve the charted lists and date-stamp them, because sometimes the conflict is between institutions, not within the household.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Exactly, and I think we should make the medication timeline a shared artifact. The discharge list, what reconciliation documented, pharmacy fill or substitution if we can get it, the first outpatient list, and then the separate household accounts. That lets us distinguish an actual home-management change from, say, an EHR carry-forward problem. I still need analytics to tell me whether the fill feed has enough turnaround for that to be useful in real- in real time.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Patel
transcript.text: Mm, the turnaround is key.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Morales
transcript.text: And on the qualitative side, a retrospective feed could still be useful even if it can't guide the immediate contact. It gives us a way to ask whether what looks like a household medication change was actually a substitution, a delayed fill, or something that never became available. But we'd need to be careful not to let the fill record stand in for what people understood they were taking.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: And I’d keep those sources distinct rather than treating any one as the ground truth. For the clinical endpoint, though, we need the dates anchored, anchored to discharge, reconciliation, fills if available, outpatient review, and any readmission. That timeline is probably the bridge between what Rafael’s hearing and what we can defensibly call medication adherence or a transition failure.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Morales
transcript.text: The timeline is also where we need to guard against making the causal story too tidy. A dated fill or a completed call tells us something happened, but not necessarily whether the household could actually carry out the plan. For the protocol, I want the interview prompts and observation notes tied to those same dates, so we can ask what changed around each handoff instead of asking for a general account of adherence.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: That works for me. If the prompts are anchored to the actual handoffs, we may be able to separate a true implementation failure, where nobody could obtain or interpret the medication, from a list-management problem in the EHR. I’ll make sure the clinical specification preserves those dates and source labels. Assuming analytics can give us the fill data with enough completeness, I’ll— actually, that’s the condition for making that distinction.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Patel
transcript.text: For the costing, I need those source labels carried through too, because an apparent medication failure can generate very different downstream work. A quick clarification call versus repeated pharmacy, outpatient, and community-navigation contacts. Maya, when analytics comes back, could we also pin down whether we get utilization beyond our own hospital? I was thinking at least claims-level ED and readmission use. Otherwise we risk calling something avoided when it was just displaced.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Morales
transcript.text: Hm, that’s an important distinction.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: I'll ask analytics specifically about cross-system utilization, and what the lag and completeness look like for claims versus our internal ADT data. I don't want 30-day all-cause readmission to quietly become— I mean, "readmission here," especially if the navigation is changing where people seek care rather than whether they need it.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Patel
transcript.text: Right, I’d want that completeness.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Morales
transcript.text: Yes—otherwise we may be measuring displacement rather than reduced need.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Exactly. I’ll put both internal ADT and any available claims-based utilization into the analytics questions, and spell out the refresh lag. Until we know that, I think in the draft we should call the endpoint internal-hospital readmission rather than imply we have complete 30-day capture, because...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Morales
transcript.text: That wording is important for the interview materials too. We should not let participants infer that a return elsewhere is somehow outside the study's account of what happened. I can make the prompts ask broadly about urgent care, emergency visits, and, and hospital use after discharge, while keeping their narrative separate from the administrative endpoint.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: That’s a good safeguard. I’ll keep the administrative endpoint explicitly labeled as internal-hospital capture while we’re waiting on the claims answer, and Rafael’s broader utilization prompts can sit alongside it instead of being folded into the readmission variable.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Aisha Patel
transcript.text: Okay, I think that’s enough for today. We covered what I needed. Thanks, both. We can pick this back up once Maya’s heard from analytics.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Sounds good. Bye, both.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Rafael Morales
transcript.text: All right. Take care, both.
